authorship: Twenty user-supplied questions frozen verbatim; two agent-authored unsupported controls clearly separated.
label_provenance: Agent source review before model outputs; not independent human gold labels.

cases.query: What happens to running applications if a Kubernetes Deployment is deleted?

source_evidence.text: By default, deleting the Deployment also deletes its running Pods, causing downtime

cases.scope_note: Orphan deletion is a documented exception; do not assert unconditional deletion for every cascading policy.

cases.query: How does Kubernetes handle a failed application pod in a Deployment?

source_evidence.text: If you manually delete a Pod, the lifecycle is controlled by the ReplicaSet and the replacement will be created immediately
Only a .spec.template.spec.restartPolicy equal to Always is allowed

cases.scope_note: Failure may mean a container crash or a deleted/failed Pod. The source establishes Always restartPolicy and ReplicaSet replacement for deletion; do not claim every crash necessarily creates a new Pod or rolls back a bad release.

cases.query: Can I roll back a Deployment after a bad application update?

source_evidence.text: Rollback to an earlier Deployment revision if the current state of the Deployment is not stable.
Sometimes, you may want to rollback a Deployment; for example, when the Deployment is not stable, such as crash looping.

cases.query: How can I update my application without causing downtime?

source_evidence.text: A new ReplicaSet is created, and the Deployment gradually scales it up while scaling down the old ReplicaSet
It does not kill old Pods until a sufficient number of new Pods have come up

cases.scope_note: Availability depends on configuration, readiness and application capacity; a generic unconditional zero-downtime guarantee is not established.

cases.query: When should I use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?

source_evidence.text: stable is synonymous with persistence across Pod (re)scheduling.

If an application doesn't require any stable identifiers or ordered deployment, deletion, or scaling, you should deploy your application using a workload object that provides a set of stateless replicas.

cases.query: If a StatefulSet pod crashes, will it keep the same identity?

source_evidence.text: the persistent Pod identifiers make it easier to match existing volumes to the new Pods that replace any that have failed.
The identity sticks to the Pod, regardless of which node it's (re)scheduled on.

cases.query: Does each StatefulSet pod get its own persistent storage?

source_evidence.text: For each VolumeClaimTemplate entry defined in a StatefulSet, each Pod receives one PersistentVolumeClaim.

cases.scope_note: Do not claim every StatefulSet automatically has persistent storage without configured/provisioned volumes.

cases.query: Can StatefulSet pods be scaled down in any order?

source_evidence.text: When Pods are being deleted, they are terminated in reverse order, from {N-1..0}.
Parallel pod management tells the StatefulSet controller to launch or terminate all Pods in parallel

cases.query: How can I run a monitoring agent on every Kubernetes node?

source_evidence.text: A DaemonSet ensures that all (or some) Nodes run a copy of a Pod.

cases.query: What happens when I add another node to a cluster that uses a DaemonSet?

source_evidence.text: As nodes are added to the cluster, Pods are added to them.

cases.query: How can I stop a DaemonSet from running on certain nodes?

source_evidence.text: If you specify a .spec.template.spec.nodeSelector, then the DaemonSet controller will create Pods on nodes which match that node selector.
Likewise if you specify a .spec.template.spec.affinity, then DaemonSet controller will create Pods on nodes which match that node affinity.

cases.query: What happens to DaemonSet pods when their nodes become unavailable?

source_evidence.text: | node.kubernetes.io/not-ready | NoExecute | DaemonSet Pods can be scheduled onto nodes that are not healthy or ready to accept Pods. Any DaemonSet Pods running on such nodes will not be evicted. |

| node.kubernetes.io/unreachable | NoExecute | DaemonSet Pods can be scheduled onto nodes that are unreachable from the node controller. Any DaemonSet Pods running on such nodes will not be evicted. |

cases.scope_note: Unreachable is not the same as a node being removed; removed-node Pods are garbage-collected. No source establishes that a DaemonSet automatically moves the same Pod to a different node.

cases.query: How do Kubernetes Services find the correct application pods?

source_evidence.text: The set of Pods targeted by a Service is usually determined by a selector that you define.
The controller for that Service continuously scans for Pods that match its selector

cases.query: What's the difference between ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer?

source_evidence.text: ClusterIP: Exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP.
NodePort: Exposes the Service on each Node's IP at a static port (the NodePort).
LoadBalancer: Exposes the Service externally using an external load balancer.

cases.query: If a pod's IP address changes, will its Service still work?

source_evidence.text: While the actual Pods that compose the backend set may change, the frontend clients should not need to be aware of that
Kubernetes updates the EndpointSlices for a Service whenever the set of Pods in a Service changes.

cases.query: Can a Kubernetes Service route traffic to pods in another namespace?

source_evidence.text: You want to point your Service to a Service in a different Namespace or on another cluster.
An ExternalName Service is a special case of Service that does not have selectors and uses DNS names instead.

cases.scope_note: The question is broader than automatic selector-based discovery. Do not reduce it to an unconditional no; the article explicitly discusses cross-namespace Service indirection.

cases.query: What's the difference between an Ingress and a LoadBalancer Service?

source_evidence.text: Ingress exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services within the cluster.
LoadBalancer: Exposes the Service externally using an external load balancer.

cases.query: Can one Ingress expose multiple applications using different URL paths?

source_evidence.text: A fanout configuration routes traffic from a single IP address to more than one Service, based on the HTTP URI being requested.

cases.query: Does creating an Ingress automatically make my application accessible?

source_evidence.text: You must have an Ingress controller to satisfy an Ingress. Only creating an Ingress resource has no effect.

cases.query: What should I check if my Ingress returns a 404 error?

source_evidence.text: Both the host and path must match the content of an incoming request before the load balancer directs traffic to the referenced Service.
A backend is a combination of Service and port names as described in the Service doc
If defaultBackend is not set, the handling of requests that do not match any of the rules will be up to the ingress controller

cases.scope_note: The article does not explicitly document HTTP 404 diagnosis. Routing checks are source-supported guidance, not a confirmed diagnosis; controller-specific troubleshooting needs additional evidence. Scope is reviewable.

cases.scope_note: Supplemental control, not part of the twenty user-supplied questions; static official docs do not establish live cluster values.
